en: The Jātaka,
Great Collection, Chapter on the Mūgapakkha (The Dumb and Paralysed)
7. The Birth Story of Prince Candaka:
You were once a king of cruel deeds, the sole ruler of Pupphavatī.
Thus he questioned the fallen Brahmin,
the deluded court priest Khaṇḍahāla:
“Explain the path to the heavenly realms.”
“You are a brahmin skilled in the Dhamma and Vinaya;
[explain] how people, having performed meritorious deeds, go from here to a happy destination.”
“Having given excessive gifts,
and having caused those who should not be slain to be killed,
in this way they go to a happy destination.”
“Having performed meritorious deeds,
men [attain heaven]. But what is that supreme gift,
and who are those who are not to be slain in this world?”
"But tell us this:
how shall I sacrifice? I will give gifts.
"O King, one should sacrifice with one's sons."
“O King, one should sacrifice with the fourfold set: with mahesīs, with merchants,
with bulls, and with thoroughbred horses.”
Having heard that, in the inner palace,
the cry arose: "Let the princes and the chief queens be slain!"—
it was a single sound.
A loud cry arose from Bhīṣmā:
“Go and speak to the princes—
Canda, Sūriya, and Bhaddasena!”
Sūra and Vāmagotta,
you should indeed be numerous for the sake of the sacrifice;
speak also to the young maidens.
Upasena, Kokila, and Mudita;
and Nandā the young maiden as well—
you were indeed numerous for the sake of sacrifice.
And my great mares— Erāvatī,
Kesinī, and Sunandā— were endowed with the most excellent marks.
"Be diligent indeed for the sake of the sacrifice.
And tell the householders:
'Puṇṇamukha, Bhaddiya, and Siṅgāla.'"
"And to the householder Vaḍḍha,
you indeed became numerous for the sake of the sacrifice.
Thus, those householders there—
Having assembled, surrounded by their wives and children, they said:
"O King, let us all become ascetics,
or else proclaim us as your slaves."
“Bring quickly those two elephants,
Abhayaṅkara and Nāḷāgiri, who are towering and have tusks like Varuṇa’s.”
For the sake of sacrifice there will be the horse-treasure Kesi, Surāmukha, Puṇṇaka, and Vinataka.
Bring them quickly,
for they will serve for sacrifice:
even the bull, the leader of the herd, Anoja.
"Bring me also that bull Nisabha, the lord of cattle;
let them assemble everything,
for I shall perform a sacrifice and give gifts."
Prepare everything for the sacrifice when the sun has risen,
and give orders to the princes.
Enjoy this night.
Perform all [the rites] when the sun has risen.
"Now speak to the princes;
today is indeed the last night.
Thus his mother spoke to each one.
Weeping, they came from the celestial mansion and said:
"O son, it is said that a sacrifice will be performed by you with your four sons."
“All my sons have been sacrificed when the moon was being slain;
having performed a sacrifice with my sons, [I shall now offer myself].”
“I shall go to a happy destination, to heaven.
“Do not believe that, my son; it is said that a happy destination is attained by means of a sacrifice of one’s own son.”
This path leads to hell;
it is not the path to the heavens.
Give gifts, Koṇḍañña!
Non-violence toward all living beings—
this is the path to a happy destination;
it is not the path through the sacrifice of one's children.
“By the word of my teachers,
I shall slay both the moon and the sun;
having performed a sacrifice with sons who are so difficult to give away.”
“I shall go to a happy destination, to heaven.
His father, Vasavatti, spoke thus to his own legitimate son.
“Indeed, my son, you shall perform a sacrifice with four sons.
“All of my sons are indeed four.”
While the moon is being slaughtered,
having performed a sacrifice with my sons,
I shall go to a good destination, to heaven.”
“Do not believe that, my son, that there is a happy destination for one who offers a sacrifice of a son;
this is a path leading to hell.”
For this is not the path to the heavenly realms.
Give gifts, Koṇḍañña;
non-violence is for the welfare of all living beings.
This is the path to a happy rebirth;
it is not the path by means of a sacrifice of sons.
[It is] from the words of the teachers.
I shall strike down both the moon and the sun;
having performed a sacrifice with my sons— those so difficult to give away—
I shall go to a happy destination, to heaven.”
“Give gifts, Koṇḍañña!
Non-violence toward all beings is for their welfare;
surrounded by your sons, you—”
“Protect the kingdom and the countryside.
“Do not kill us, O King;
give us as slaves to Khaṇḍahāla!”
We are even those who bind with chains;
we tend elephants and horses.
O King, do not put us to death.
Give us to Khaṇḍahāla as slaves;
even if bound in chains,
we would cast off the elephant goads.
O God, do not kill us;
give us to the slave Khaṇḍahāla!
Even as those bound in iron chains—
Let us cast away the horse's fodder.
O King, do not slay us;
give us as slaves to Khaṇḍahāla.
“Since you have these desires,
even though you have been exiled from the kingdom,
we shall go forth as wanderers for alms.”
“You cause me suffering indeed with these lamentations, for you desire life;
release the princes now!”
“Let there be some small portion for me from the sacrifice of your son.
“I have already told you before:
this is difficult to do and hard to accomplish.”
Now that our sacrifice has been prepared,
why do you cause its interruption?
All shall go to a happy destination.
Those who sacrifice, those who cause sacrifices to be performed,
and those who rejoice in such a great sacrifice as this performed by these sacrificers.
“Then why did people formerly invoke blessings for safety upon brahmins? And now,
for no reason at all, [they do so for us].”
O King, you slaughtered us for the sake of sacrifice;
yet previously, when we were still children,
you neither struck nor killed us.
Having passed from childhood into youth,
O father, we were innocent; yet we were slain,
whether mounted on elephants or horses.
Behold us, O Great King, when we are armored,
whether engaged in battle or preparing for war;
for men like us do not become heroes for the sake of sacrifice.
Or when the borderlands are in revolt,
or in the forests, they employ men like us;
yet for us, there is no cause [for such service].
We would be killed, dear father, on an unsuitable ground.
For even those birds that dwell having made their homes of grass, [are destroyed when caught in snares].
Even their dear sons—
those you have caused us to lose, O King.
Do not believe his words.
Khaṇḍahāla would not kill me;
for having killed me, O King,
he would kill him immediately thereafter.
They give excellent villages, excellent towns,
and even great wealth, O Great King;
and even a mere morsel of food—
They eat from this house and that house;
even toward such as these,
O Great King, they desire to commit treachery.
For the most part,
O King, these brahmins are ungrateful;
do not slay us, O King.
"Give us to Khaṇḍahāla as slaves!
Even though we are bound in chains,
we shall guard the elephants and horses."
"O God, do not kill us!
Give us to the slave Khaṇḍahāla;
even as those bound in iron chains,"
"Let us cast off these elephant-ornaments!
O King, do not kill us;
give us as slaves to Khaṇḍahāla."
Even if we were bound in iron chains,
O King, let us cast away the fodder for our horses;
do not put us to death.
"O slave, give us to Khaṇḍahāla;
even though you have been exiled from the kingdom, let those who desire you have them."
“We shall go on the alms-round.
“You cause me pain indeed,
lamenting though you desire life.”
“Release the princes now;
let there be enough for me with this sacrifice of sons.
“I have already told you before:”
"This is difficult to do and hard to accomplish;
why then do you cause a disturbance regarding our prepared sacrifice?"
All go to a happy destination:
those who sacrifice, those who cause others to sacrifice,
and those who rejoice in the merit.
"For those who perform such a great sacrifice as this.
"If indeed, having sacrificed with their sons,
they go from here to the world of the gods upon passing away;"
"Let the brahmin perform the sacrifice first;
afterwards, you too shall sacrifice as king.
If, indeed, having sacrificed with your sons,"
Having passed away from here, they go to the world of the gods;
this indeed is Khaṇḍahāla’s sacrifice,
performed with his own sons as the victims.
Knowing this, Khaṇḍahāla,
why did you not kill your own children and all your kinsmen?
And you did not harm yourself.
All those who sacrifice and those who cause others to sacrifice go to hell.
And those who rejoice in such a great sacrifice being offered by others—
if indeed he who kills is purified [by it], then...
Even after death, he goes to a heavenly state;
for they who address others as "friend" might kill those who address them as "friend," and those who would believe their words [would likewise suffer].
And how is it, householders,
that wives desiring sons do not petition the king in the city?
"Do not kill your own dear son.
How indeed, O householders,
do wives who desire sons [act]?
In the city, they did not cry out to the king,
“Do not kill your own son, your child!”; rather,
I was one who desired the king’s welfare.
And he is beloved by all the people;
no one feels aversion toward him,
nor does anyone report anything against him to me.
"Go, my wives, and tell both your husband and Khaṇḍahāla:
'Do not kill the princes!'"
"Go to your wives, who resemble lions that have committed no offense,
and speak to them, as well as to my father and Khaṇḍahāla."
"Do not kill the princes;
they are beloved by the whole world.
What if I were to give birth?"
Or among chariot-maker families,
or among scavenger families, or among the merchant class— I would have been born there,
and thus the king would not have had me executed at the sacrifice.”
“All you women with parted hair, go to the noble Khaṇḍahāla;
fall at his feet.”
"I see no offense.
All you women with parted hair, go to the noble Khaṇḍahāla."
“Fall at his feet;
what have we, venerable sir, done to offend you?
Thus Selā wailed piteously.
Having seen that his brothers had been brought forward,
he thought: "It seems my father,
desiring heaven, has canceled my sacrifice."
Āvatti, Parivatti, Vasula,
and Sammukhā said to the king:
"Do not kill our father."
"From childhood we have reached youth.
"This, Vasula, is your father;
greet him together with your father."
"You cause me suffering indeed,
lamenting thus within the inner palace;
release the princes now!"
“Let there be some reward for me from the sacrifice of my son.
“I have already told you before:
this is difficult to do and hard to accomplish.”
Now that our sacrifice has been prepared,
why do you cause this distraction?
All shall go to a happy destination.
Those who sacrifice, those who cause others to sacrifice,
and those who rejoice in such a great sacrifice of those who are sacrificing.
The sacrifice of all treasures has been prepared,
O sole king, it is ready for you; go forth, O Lord!
Having gone to heaven, you will rejoice.
These seven hundred young women are the wives of Prince Canda.
Tearing at their hair,
they followed along the road weeping; others,
however, out of grief, [did likewise].
Like gods departing from the Nandana grove,
they followed along the road, weeping and disheveling their hair.
“Wearing fine garments of Kāsī cloth,
adorned with earrings and anointed with aloe-wood and sandalwood,
the moon and sun go forth.”
For the sake of sacrifice for the sole monarch:
wearing fine garments of Kāsī cloth,
adorned with earrings, and anointed with aloe and sandalwood;
The moon and the sun pass away,
having caused grief to their mother's heart;
they depart wearing garments of pure Kāsī cloth.
Adorned with earrings and anointed with agaru and sandalwood,
the moon and sun set forth,
causing heart-rending grief for the people.
Those who eat meat broth, those bathed and well-groomed by barbers,
adorned with earrings and anointed with agaru and sandalwood—
these are led forth like the moon and the sun.
For the sake of the sacrifice of the sole king,
there were bathers and barbers who fed on meat and broth,
adorned with earrings and anointed with aloe-wood and sandalwood.
The moon and sun depart,
leaving behind the heartache of their mother;
they were nourished on meat broth and bathed by their nurses and daughters-in-law.
Anointed with agaru and sandalwood,
the moon and sun go forth,
causing heart-rending grief for the people.
Those who formerly followed on foot behind those mounted upon the backs of elephants,
even the moon and sun must now leave them here.
Both go on foot.
Those who formerly followed those excellent steeds when they had mounted their backs now follow behind on horses.
Let go of the moon and the sun;
both have gone on foot.
Those who formerly stood at the yoke of the best of chariots—
They follow on chariots;
there, both the moon and the sun go on foot.
In former times, they used to travel by means of swift horses equipped with harnesses that cause them to burn with speed;
but now, the moon and the sun—
"Both go on foot. "If you,
bird, desire meat, fly before Pupphavatī."
There, the sole ruler,
being utterly deluded by his four sons,
sacrifices; if you desire meat, O bird, [then eat].
Be gracious to Puṣpavatī as before;
let the sole ruler sacrifice here,
for he is bewildered by the four maidens.
If you, bird, desire meat, fly to the east of Pupphavatī;
there the sole monarch performs sacrifice.
He was utterly bewildered by the four great queens.
"If you, O bird, desire meat, fly to the east of Pupphavatī."
Let the sole ruler here perform the sacrifice,
though he is deluded by the four householders.
If you desire the flesh of a bird, [then let him do so].
Be gracious to Puṣpavatī’s father;
let the sole king sacrifice here,
for he has become bewildered by the four elephants.
If you, O bird, desire meat, fly to the east of Pupphavatī;
there the sole king performs sacrifice.
He was utterly bewildered by the four horses.
"If you, O bird, desire my flesh,
fly toward the east of Pupphavatī."
Let the sole ruler sacrifice here;
he is bewildered by four bulls.
If you, O bird, desire meat, [let him sacrifice].
"Be gracious to Puṣpavatī from the east;
let the sole king sacrifice here,
for he is utterly bewildered by the fourfold [set]."
This is his palace,
this inner apartment is most delightful;
now, O noble sons, [enter].
Four were led away for execution.
This was his gabled house,
covered with golden flowers and strewn with garlands.
"Now, noble sons,
these four have been led away for execution.
This is his pleasure grove."
That delightful grove, which blooms at all times throughout the year—
therein, O noble sons,
you four have now been led away for execution.
This is his Ashoka grove,
ever-blossoming, delightful at all times;
come now, noble sons!
Four have been led away to their execution.
This is his *kaṇikāra* grove,
ever-blooming and delightful at all times.
Now, noble sons,
these four have been led away for execution.
This is his Pāṭalīvana grove.
It was in full bloom at all times, delightful;
yet now, O noble sons,
these four have been led away to execution.
This mango grove of his is in full bloom at all times, delightful;
come now, sons of noble family!
Four were led away for execution.
This is his lotus pond,
covered with pink and white lotuses.
And this ship, fashioned of gold,
adorned with flowering vines, and most delightful—
this, O noble sons, is now [yours].
Four were led away for execution.
This was his elephant-treasure:
the mighty tusker Erāvaṇa.
"Now, noble sirs,
these four have been led away for execution.
This is his horse-treasure."
The horse has a single hoof;
now, O noble sons,
four have been led away to their execution.
This is his horse-chariot,
Sāḷiya, a beautiful sound, variegated with jewels;
wherein the noble sons [dwell].
They shone like gods in the Nandana grove;
yet now these four noble sons have been led away for execution.
How indeed will the king perform the sacrifice with those who are as beautiful as the moon and whose limbs are as soft as sandalwood?
He was utterly bewildered by his four sons—
those who were as beautiful as Sāma,
with limbs as soft as sandalwood.
The king, being utterly deluded, will perform a sacrifice with four maidens;
how indeed can he do so with those who are as beautiful as Sāmā?
With bodies fragrant with sandalwood,
the king, utterly deluded, will perform a sacrifice together with his four chief queens.
How indeed will the king perform the sacrifice with those who are as beautiful as the moon and whose limbs are as soft as sandalwood?
He was bewildered by four householders:
"Just as villages and market towns may be empty,
devoid of human beings, and vast wildernesses [may be likewise]."
"So it shall be for Pupphavatī, during the auspicious conjunctions of the moon and sun.
"I shall become mad; I will go insane."
Though trampled by the earth and covered with dust,
if it should strike the excellent moon,
O King, my very life-breaths would be cut off.
I shall become insane,
struck down and covered with dust,
if I kill the noble sun.
“O King, my lives are being cut short.
“Why indeed would they not find delight,
speaking kindly to one another?”
The boatman’s wife, the overseer,
the pond-keeper, and the heavy-laden woman— these four dance before the moon and the sun.
“Among them, no equality exists.
“Let Khaṇḍahāla’s mother take upon herself this grief of my heart;”
This grief in my heart,
[arising] when the moon was led out for execution—
this grief in my heart, [I shall now dispel].
Let your mother, Khaṇḍahāla, fasten it on herself;
let her wear that grief in her heart which I have when you are led away for execution under the sun.
Let Khaṇḍahāla’s wife take upon herself this sorrow of my heart—
this sorrow of my heart that I have.
Now that Canda has been led away for execution,
let Khaṇḍahāla’s wife take upon herself this grief of my heart.
The grief in my heart,
when the sun was led forth for execution—
do not [grieve] for sons, do not for a husband.
Khaṇḍahāla, your mother saw him—
him whom you had caused to be slain,
though he was innocent and like a lion.
Neither her sons nor her husband did your mother see, O Khaṇḍahāla,
when you had those princes slain.
"Disregarded by the whole world,
O Khaṇḍahāla, your wife has seen neither her son nor her husband."
You who have slain the princes,
who were innocent and like lions—
do not [grieve for] your sons, nor for your husband.
Khaṇḍahāla, your wife has seen him—
the one whom you had the princes killed while they were being watched by the whole world.
“O Lord, do not kill us!
Give us to Khaṇḍahāla the slave.
Even if we are bound in fetters, [we shall serve you].”
"We tend the elephants and horses.
O King, do not kill us;
give us to Khaṇḍahāla as his slaves."
Even if we were bound in iron chains,
we would cast off the elephant goads;
O King, do not put us to death.
"Give us to Khaṇḍahāla as slaves;
even if we are bound in chains,
we shall at least cast off the fodder of the horses."
O God, do not slay us;
give us as slaves to Khaṇḍahāla,
to whom your desires belong.
Even though we have been banished from our kingdom,
we shall go about for alms;
O King, they pray for divine [boons].
Some women, though desiring sons and being poor, lose their eloquence and do not obtain children.
They offer blessings, saying:
"May sons be born to us, and from them, grandsons;
then, for no reason..."
O King, you have slaughtered him for the sake of a sacrifice.
People obtain a son through prayers;
do not, my dear father, bring us misfortune.
Do not perform this sacrifice with sons obtained through hardship;
people obtain a son by means of prayers for a boon.
Do not, dear father,
cause us grief; do not separate us from our mother with sons who have obtained so little.
Having raised me with great hardship,
O mother, you have grown old because of your son;
I indeed bow at your feet.
"Father, may you attain the world beyond.
Now, embrace me and let me,
mother, pay homage at your feet."
Now I am going abroad for the sake of a sacrifice for the sole monarch;
come now, embrace me.
"Mother, give me leave to pay homage at your feet;
I am now going abroad,
leaving heartache for my mother."
Now, embrace me and grant me leave to worship at your feet, mother;
I am now departing on a journey abroad.
Causing grief in the hearts of the people.
"Come now, son of Gotamī, bind a wreath of lotus petals; [place it upon my head]."
This admixture of campaka petals is your ancient nature; here,
take this ointment for you.
Anoint yourself with the finest sandalwood paste,
so that, well-anointed,
you may shine resplendent in the assembly of kings.
Now, take these soft garments and clothe yourself in this fine Kāsī cloth;
well-dressed in these, [you shall go].
You shine in the assembly of kings.
Take these hand-ornaments, adorned with pearls, gems, and gold.
"And with these hand-ornaments you shine in the assembly of kings.
"Surely this is not Raṭṭhapāla; [it must be someone else]."
The lord of the earth is the heir of the realm;
the great ruler of the world conceives affection for his sons.
“Sons are dear to me too, and I am dear to you, my wives; and I,
longing for heaven, [shall go there].”
"Therefore, I shall have you killed. "Kill me first;
do not tear at my heart with grief."
O King, your son Sundaraka is adorned and delicate;
therefore, O Lord, slay me instead.
"In the next world, I shall be with Candaka;
perform abundant merit,
so that we both may wander together in the next world."
“O Candi, do not find death pleasing;
you have many divine husbands, O large-eyed one;
they will delight you.”
When it was said, "In the sacrifice of Gotamiputta," Canda struck herself with her palms.
“What is the use of life here?
I shall drink poison; I will die.
Surely this king—”
There are indeed dear friends who do not say to the king,
"Do not kill your own sons."
Surely this king has relatives and friends who are well-disposed toward him,
for those who do not speak out to the king [must exist].
"Do not kill your own sons.
These too are my sons,
O King— virtuous and wearing golden armlets."
Offer the sacrifice even with those;
then let him release the son of Gotamī.
Having made me a hundred pits, [let him do so].
Sacrifice [him], O Great King, dividing him into seven parts;
do not slay your eldest son,
who is innocent and as majestic as a lion.
O Great King, having made me your companion, perform the sacrifice sevenfold;
do not slay your eldest son.
"Desired by the whole world.
"Many were the various ornaments given to you for your well-spoken words;"
“Pearls, gems, and beryl—
this is your final gift.
“For those whose aggregates in the past...”
The flower garlands have fallen away;
even their well-sharpened stalks will fall from the trunks.
For those whose minds, like garlands of flowers, formerly unfurled upon the aggregates— even now, for them,
the well-sharpened [arrow]...
The spearhead will be turned away from their aggregates.
Indeed, before long,
O princes, the spearhead will be turned away from their aggregates.
Then my heart did not break;
until that time, it remained firmly bound.
Clad in fine garments of Kāsī cloth,
Adorned with earrings and anointed with agarwood and sandalwood,
go forth, O Moon and Sun,
for the sake of the sacrifice of the sole king.
Wearing fine garments of Kāsī cloth,
adorned with earrings and anointed with aloe-wood and sandalwood,
go forth like the moon and the sun.
Having caused grief to their mother’s heart, they—
wearing pure garments of Kāsī cloth, adorned with earrings,
and anointed with agaru and sandalwood paste— set out.
Depart, O Moon and Sun,
having caused heartache for the people.
You who feed on meat broth, you who are bathed and groomed— depart!
Adorned with earrings and anointed with agarwood and sandalwood,
go forth, O Moon and Sun,
for the sake of the sacrifice of the sole monarch.
Feasting on meat broth, bathed and well-anointed,
adorned with earrings and smeared with aloe and sandalwood paste—
go forth, O Moon and Sun!
Having caused grief to his mother’s heart,
he was fed with meat broth, bathed by his daughter-in-law,
adorned with earrings, and anointed with agaru and sandalwood.
Depart, O Moon and Sun,
having caused heart-grief for the people!
For everything has been prepared.
When the moon had set for the sake of the sacrifice,
the daughter of the King of Pañcāla, with palms joined in reverence,
walked around the entire assembly.
“By that truth by which the foolish Khaṇḍahāla commits evil deeds— by this utterance of truth,
[may he be released].”
I am united with my husband.
Whatever non-human beings there are here,
and whatever yakkhas, bhūtas, or bhavyas;
May you grant me your assistance;
may I be united with my husband.
Whatever deities have come here—
And whatever spirits, ghosts, or bhūtas there may be:
protect me, who am helpless and seeking refuge;
I entreat you, O husband, that I may not be defeated.”
Having heard that, the non-human being,
having whirled around an iron mace while instilling fear in him, [struck him].
He said this to the king:
“Awake, O wretched king!
Do not let me strike you on the crown of your head.”
Do not kill your eldest son,
who is innocent and like a lion.
What wicked king have you seen, O King?
Wives and children are being slaughtered,
as are the wealthy householders;
for they are innocent and desire heaven.
Having heard that and having seen this marvel, both Khaṇḍahāla and the king released all their bonds.
So that there was no harm done to any of those who had gathered there at that time, having been set free from all [bonds].
Everyone threw a single clod of earth;
this was the execution of Khaṇḍahāla.
They all entered hell.
Just as it is for one who has committed an evil deed: for having performed an evil action,
it is not possible to go from here to a happy destination.
When all those who had gathered there at that time were fully liberated,
they consecrated the Moon.
And the royal assembly gathered there.
When all were fully liberated,
those who had assembled there at that time—
The assembled royal maidens consecrated Canda; when all were liberated,
[he was released].
Those who were assembled there at that time—
the gathered assembly of gods— consecrated the Moon.
When all those who had gathered there at that time were fully liberated,
they consecrated the Moon.
And the daughters of the gods gathered there as well.
When all those who had assembled there at that time were fully liberated, [the world was filled with joy].
The assembled royal retinue broke into loud laughter; when they were all released,
[the king] was filled with joy.
Those who were assembled there at that time,
as well as the gathered princesses, raised their garments in a gesture of protest.
When all had been liberated,
those who were assembled there at that time raised their garments in a gesture of joy.
And the assembly of devas gathered there.
When all were fully liberated,
those who had assembled there at that time—
The assembled daughters of the gods also raised a great cry; when all were thus liberated,
[the world rejoiced].
I was greatly delighted;
I entered the city in joy, proclaiming,
"Liberation from bonds has been announced!"
The Candakumāra Jātaka, the seventh.
